name: Fucoidan
lead: Fucoidan is a group of sulfated polysaccharides, built largely from the sugar fucose, found in the cell walls of brown seaweeds and in a few marine invertebrates such as sea cucumbers and sea urchins.[1][2][3] Commercial material is usually extracted from species including Fucus vesiculosus, Laminaria japonica (kombu), Undaria pinnatifida (wakame) and Cladosiphon okamuranus.[1] Its structure varies with species, season and extraction method, which makes products hard to compare.[3][5]

It is sold as a dietary supplement, food additive and cosmetic ingredient, and appears in the longevity-supplement category as a general-purpose marine extract.[1] Laboratory work has reported anti-inflammatory, anticoagulant, antiviral, antioxidant and antitumour activity in cells and animals.[3][4][8][9]

Wikipedia states that, as of its 2019-era sources, the evidence consisted of laboratory studies, early-stage trials and case reports, that no advanced clinical trials had been reported, and that no national regulator had designated it safe for human use.[1] No published study found in these sources tests fucoidan for facial appearance, skin ageing or any other cosmetic outcome.

paras: Fucoidan is a heterogeneous mixture rather than a single molecule. The backbone is typically alpha-linked L-fucose carrying sulfate ester groups, with galactose, mannose, xylose, glucose and uronic acids present in varying proportions depending on the seaweed.[2][3] Reported molecular weights span from tens of kilodaltons to over a million daltons.[2] Reviews of structure-function work note that sulfate content, molecular weight and extraction method all influence measured bioactivity, and that the difficulty of standardising these features complicates comparison between studies.[5][3]

Fucoidan was first isolated from brown algae in the early twentieth century; the Swedish scientist Harald Kylin described it in 1913 under the name fucoidin.[1][2] Methods for laboratory extraction were established later, and Wikipedia reports that it became commercially available in the 1970s.[1] A 1993 paper in the Journal of Biological Chemistry proposed a revised structure for fucoidan that its authors suggested could explain some of its biological activities.[17]

A comparative study of nine fucoidans from different brown algae found that all inhibited leukocyte recruitment in a rat inflammation model and reported differing anticoagulant, antiangiogenic and antiadhesive activity between sources.[4] A 1988 study reported that sulfated polysaccharides inhibited several enveloped viruses in cell culture.[8] Sulfated polysaccharide fractions from Laminaria japonica showed antioxidant activity in laboratory assays.[16] These findings come from cell and animal work; they do not by themselves establish effects in people.

Human research is limited to small, mostly registered trials, largely of an oligo-fucoidan preparation, in medical conditions rather than appearance. Registered studies include one in active rheumatoid arthritis (recruiting, 40 participants),[6] one in cancer cachexia and sarcopenia (100),[7] one on radiation lung damage (100),[11] a terminated study in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (87),[9] a small early-phase study in uterine leiomyoma (18),[10] and a study listed under ageing that targets the longevity-associated protein SIRT6 (60, recruiting).[12] A withdrawn trial in lung cancer patients receiving chemotherapy never enrolled.[13] The sources consulted report no completed randomised trial showing a benefit for a cosmetic or ageing outcome.

Wikipedia states that evidence for safe use is limited and that product quality varies widely.[1] Fucoidan has anticoagulant properties in laboratory tests.[4] Seaweed-derived products can also contain variable levels of iodine and heavy metals; brown algae are known to concentrate heavy metals from seawater.[14]

It is sold in Southeast Asia and elsewhere as a supplement, and appears in combination joint products on the US market alongside glucosamine and collagen.[15] Wikipedia reports it is recognised as a natural health product in Canada but has not been approved as a human drug in any country.[1]

timeline.event: Harald Kylin isolates the polysaccharide from brown algae and names it fucoidin.[1][2]

card.summary: A brown-seaweed sulfated sugar sold as a longevity supplement; lab results are plentiful, human appearance data absent.
card.note: Not approved as a drug anywhere; products vary widely in composition.

quick.overview:
Fucoidan is a family of sulfated polysaccharides extracted from brown seaweeds such as kombu and wakame. It is sold as a supplement and appears in longevity-focused product lines.

Cell and animal studies report anti-inflammatory, antiviral and antioxidant activity. Human trials are small and mostly address medical conditions; none found test a cosmetic or appearance outcome.
quick.mechanism: Its bioactivity is attributed to its fucose backbone and sulfate groups, which can bind proteins involved in inflammation, clotting and viral attachment in laboratory systems. Activity depends on the seaweed source, molecular weight and extraction method.
quick.risks: Evidence for human safety is described as limited and product quality varies. It shows anticoagulant activity in lab tests, and seaweed products can carry variable iodine and metal content. It is not approved as a drug in any country.
